body:
Thanks for the issue @WilcoFiers!

The point of ElementInternals being only accessible once via `attachInternals` is that it provides private APIs designed only for the custom element author, and it is up to them to expose what they wish to. Exposing them via a property violates that design principle. Custom Element authors are aware of this and in fact rely on ElementInternals not being exposed, so exposing it (certainly exposing the ability to write to it) may cause other issues.

Given (my understanding of) the aim of axe-core is to automate accessibility testing I would offer that asking for ElementInternals to be exposed might be the wrong layer to be looking at. Perhaps more precise problem statements such as "we need to access the computed role", "we need to access the computed describedby elements" are more pointed, and perhaps better resolved in a forum like https://github.com/WICG/aom.

I recommend looking at https://github.com/whatwg/dom/issues/1290#issuecomment-2137398769 for the possible solution space here. As with shadow roots we want to preserve encapsulation here and thus cannot give unfettered access. WebDriver access seems very reasonable however.

@keithamus As I explained, a proposal for getting a [computed accessible name, role, and states exist](https://github.com/WICG/aom/issues/212). It is unlikely to ever get traction because there are significant performance problems that can occur from implementing such a proposal. It also doesn't work for tools like axe because it doesn't just need to know the end result of a computed state, it needs to know how a state is computed so it can accurately communicate why a problem occurred.

@annevk I'm not sure I understand. These tools are built to run in the DOM. How is using WebDriver a reasonable option?

I'm afraid they'll need to use an extension or some such instead then. We generally don't add APIs to the web platform solely for testing. And in this case that would also go against other goals, such as offering encapsulation.

> they'll need to use an extension or some such

That really isn't an option. Tools like ANDI and HTMLCodeSniffer are built as bookmarklets because that's often the only thing an accessibility tester is allowed to run. That work is often done on internal machines that are so locked down even installing extensions isn't possible, let alone running WebDriver.

Other DOM-anywhere tools like axe-core and Equal Access are built this way so they can be used without tying an organization to one specific testing solution. Same tool in all your browsers, your Selenium Cucumber tests, the other team's Puppeteer tests, etc. It isn't just limited to Chromium because that happens to have CDp access in its extension, or Playwright because of its accessibility tree dump. It doesn't suddenly break your accessibility tests because browser X decided that in the next version display:content elements suddenly can be in the accessibility tree or whatever.

I agree with you on the principle. it is perfectly reasonable for the DOM not to have APIs solely for the purpose of automated testing. But **accessibility testing is not automated testing**. The principle doesn't apply here. Most accessibility work is done on staging or production, by humans. This is not the same thing.

A critical issue is that it doesn't just prevent testing elements with ElementInternals. Because there's no way to check if an element has internals, every custom element has to be treated like a black box. That has implications for every custom element, as well as any element that may include a custom element in its name or any of its ARIA props. For example, there is no DOM methods that can now tell you if the following is an input with an empty label:

```html
<label>
  <my-elm></my-elm>
  <input />
</label>
```

The principle definitely applies here, it doesn't really matter if the testing is manual or automated. It's still testing. Extensions are also more interoperable now than they have ever been so I doubt a solution in that place would lock you down to any particular browser.

With all due respect, that's hardly an answer. Even if browser extension interoperability was good enough for this, which it isn't, that doesn't matter. You're completely stepping over the fact that these tools need to run in environments where getting a browser extension installed is not an option, and that `attachElementInternals` didn't just affect accessibility testing on pages that use it, but it prevents correct testing on pages that don't because there's no way to tell.

I'm just telling you that those tools will not be able to do this without some kind of non-web-exposed API, be it from an extension or WebDriver. It's very much the same as with shadow trees.

If you can guarantee the scripts of these tools run first you could patch `attachInternals()` and `attachShadow()` to workaround this to some extent perhaps.

> It's very much the same as with shadow trees.

I think shadow trees are a good comparison, but there is a critical difference between shadow trees and `ElementInternals` for this problem domain that makes it very much *not* the same: with shadow trees, authors using web components *have a choice* to allow the sort of access we're talking about to DOM-based test tools, but with `ElementInternals`, there is no such ability for an author to choose (there is no `attachInternals({ mode: 'open' })`).

This distinction is a very big deal for accessibility testing in practice; an overwhelming majority of actual shadow DOM usage today uses `mode: 'open'`, including most large web component UI frameworks/libraries. A GitHub code search suggests that the ratio of [open usage](https://github.com/search?q=%2FattachShadow%5C%28%5Cs*%5C%7B%5Cs*mode%3A+%5B%27%22%5Dopen%5B%27%22%5D%2F&type=code) to [closed usage](https://github.com/search?q=%2FattachShadow%5C%28%5Cs*%5C%7B%5Cs*mode%3A+%5B%27%22%5Dclosed%5B%27%22%5D%2F&type=code) in public GitHub projects is about **16:1**.

Would a proposal for an `attachInternals({ mode: 'open' })` interface comparable to what already exists for `attachShadow` be more palatable, perhaps? I don't think that would be any more or less "test only" than the precedent set by `attachShadow` for the same functionality, it would still meet the design goal of allowing encapsulation for those authors that want it, but in the empirically-more-common case where authors don't mind having the escape hatch, it would give authors an option that doesn't require them to rewrite their accessibility tests on top of a new test framework/architecture (which is what the "use WebDriver/an extension" option demands in practice).

It seems to me that the way you stated problem makes this problem over constrained. `ElementInternals` provide an API surface for custom element authors to access element's internal in their own accord the same way a closed shadow tree provides a way to hide the implementation details of a component.

The best way forward is probably for you to define some kind of convention that components can adhere to and rely on that convention.

> The best way forward is probably for you to define some kind of convention that components can adhere to and rely on that convention.

The specific use case in question is "tools whose primary purpose is to detect when authors have failed to follow accessibility conventions correctly." I don't think it would be a very useful way forward for tools like this to rely on authors having correctly followed an accessibility-related convention.

> > The best way forward is probably for you to define some kind of convention that components can adhere to and rely on that convention.
> 
> The specific use case in question is "tools whose primary purpose is to detect when authors have failed to follow accessibility conventions correctly." I don't think it would be a very useful way forward for tools like this to rely on authors having correctly followed an accessibility-related convention.

That problem statement is over-constrained. Such a tool cannot really exist coherently with the world in which a proper encapsulation exists for element internals.

> Such a tool cannot really exist coherently with the world in which a proper encapsulation exists

That's exactly the point. The encapsulation of element internals, without an opt out (like open shadow DOM), without even a way to detect whether internals are used, prevents correct accessibility testing of all custom elements in many of the most popular accessibility tools. So that's the request, can we come with some solution that prevents that?

Surely if we implement an opt-out but no one uses it you're left with the same problem? Or perhaps even worse, as the tooling now needs to lobby individual component authors to opt-out for their code to pass the tooling?

I am still concerned this isn't really addressing the concrete problem statement. We're one or two steps away from "I'd like to introspect the accessible role" and into "I'd like authors to opt-out of encapsulation of internals so that I can use internals to introspect the accessible role".

> Surely if we implement an opt-out but no one uses it you're left with the same problem? This is true and would be a risk, but based on current data about open vs closed shadow dom usage (where ~94% of usage is open rather than closed), we think it's likely that component authors would mostly decide in practice to use an open approach. `ElementInternals`' design has conflated "the ability to set accessibility behavior" with "the ability to *hide* that behavior from outside scripts", and we think based on the open vs closed shadow DOM statistics that most component authors that need the former probably won't care that much about the latter. I do agree that if the mechanism were strictly opt-out and defaulted to closed, this would definitely be a higher risk than with `attachShadow`, where the author needs to make an explicit choice of `mode`. > I am still concerned this isn't really addressing the concrete problem statement. We're one or two steps away from "I'd like to introspect the accessible role" and into "I'd like authors to opt-out of encapsulation of internals so that I can use internals to introspect the accessible role". This is a fair concern, and we're definitely open to alternate approaches. But I want to reiterate [the point @WilcoFiers made earlier](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11040#issuecomment-2663842234) that "I'd like to introspect the computed accessible role" is not the problem statement, either. It is not enough for accessibility testing tools to be able to query the computed accessibility properties; we need to be able to inspect *how* those properties are getting their values. There are two main reasons for this: 1. Normalizing cases where different browsers have different levels of support and would calculate computed accessibility properties differently. 2. So we can provide actionable error messages that explain what a user would actually need to change to fix an issue. I'd like to explain 1 a bit better with an example. Consider the following snippet: ```html ``` This is a real example today of a case where on the surface you'd think accessibility test tools could get away with testing the accessible names of the checkboxes by using a hypothetical `getComputedAccessibilityNode` API, but where that actually wouldn't be sufficient. First, as of writing, the stable versions of different browsers produce different output for the first checkbox (Chrome 133 says `star`, Firefox 135 says it's unlabelled). It's important for accessibility tools to be able to test the "least common denominator" behavior, regardless of what browser the tool is actually run against; it is *very common* for a specific ARIA technique to supported in some browsers and not others, and it's important that we be able to indicate a problem even if that problem might not manifest in the current browser. Here, the second checkbox (where the label comes from an `aria-label`) needs to be treated differently than the first checkbox (where the label comes from `ElementInternals`), even though some browsers would produce the same computed accessible name for both cases. Second, the first `custom-icon` doesn't actually appear in the accessibility tree (in any of Chrome/Firefox/Safari), so an approach based on checking properties of accessibility object model nodes would be problematic for us to be able to identify the source of an accessible name. This isn't a rare one-off case; this is just the first example I came up with in ~10 minutes of playing with `ElementInternals`. This pattern ("an accessibility behavior is different between browsers and we need to be able to account for those differences when doing accessibility testing") is *very common*; there are lots and lots of cases where accessibility testing tools make decisions based on "what are the different ways different browsers might handle " rather than "how would the current-browser-under-test handle ". This is the concern that is motivating us to ask for "inspecting what the user specified" rather than "inspecting what the browser calculated".

For Axe-Core or other audit frameworks specifically, there is already the ability to get some or all of what you need in a test-only context by writing a wrapper around the open-source web API audit for each of the different engine's dev tool stacks... 

For example, Safari ships with a sample Accessibility audit in the WebKit Web Inspector... What might not be as clear is that this specific "Accessibility" audit isn't intended to be a thorough as one like Axe-Core. Rather, it's intended to be sample code for audit developers like Deque for Axe-Core, so they can write and embed [their own audit in the shipping engine, or make it a downloadable, installable extension](https://webkit.org/blog/8937/creating-web-inspector-audits/)...

From #12095: there will probably be a similar issue with `referenceTarget` (https://github.com/WICG/webcomponents/blob/gh-pages/proposals/reference-target-explainer.md) where ARIA attributes are indirectly set and not exposed as DOM attributes.

I'm bringing this up because i think a solution needs to work for more than just `ElementInternals`.

@jpzwarte I think `referenceTarget` (at least as implemented in the current Chromium prototype) is actually a positive example of exactly the sort of API we're asking about - it specifically provides a standard JavaScript API (`shadowRoot.referenceTarget`) that can be queried by tools like axe-core, even within an extension content script's isolated world boundary, so long as the author has elected to use `mode: 'open'` when setting up the `shadowRoot`.

@dbjorge My viewpoint is slightly different: in component tests, i want to test that an element has an accessible name. I don't want that test to be brittle. In other words: the test should still pass after i've rewritten it from `aria-label` -> `ElementInternals` -> `referenceTarget` (just a bad example, but you get the idea).

I’m reviving this thread on behalf of the ARIA Working Group, where we’ve been actively discussing this problem. It’s becoming increasingly urgent as adoption of `ElementInternals` grows.

I originally filed a separate issue (#12095), but I’m happy to continue the discussion here.

Reading through the thread, I see three distinct objections to the original suggestion made by @WilcoFiers:
1. Exposing write access to `ElementInternals` would violate encapsulation (@keithamus)
2. The problem is over-constrained and the proposal doesn’t address the broader issue of validating author-provided accessibility semantics in closed constructs (e.g. closed shadow roots). (@rniwa)
3. This would introduce a web-exposed API purely for testing, which goes against platform principles; testing should instead be handled via WebDriver or WebExtensions. (@annevk)

I'll address each point with the goal of unblocking the discussion and identifying a viable path forward.

---
### 1. Encapsulation concerns

The concern about encapsulation is valid and well understood. The original suggestion proposed exposing a getter that returns the `ElementInternals` object itself. That would indeed undermine the core design goal of `ElementInternals`: allowing custom element authors to define internal behavior that remains hidden from consumers. Exposing a writable `ElementInternals` object would allow consumers to mutate internal state and defeat encapsulation entirely. That is not a desirable outcome.

However, I don’t believe this implies that all solutions are incompatible with encapsulation. There are alternative approaches that do not expose the internals object itself, do not allow mutation, and still address the practical accessibility testing issues described below. I’ll outline those constraints further after clarifying the scope of the problem we’re trying to solve.

---
### 2. Clarifying the problem

There is a broader, legitimate discussion to be had about whether in-page tools should be able to observe all author-provided accessibility semantics, including those inside closed constructs such as closed shadow roots. That discussion may lead to new capabilities for in-page tools, or to stronger reliance on WebDriver- or WebExtension-based solutions.

However, that is not what this issue is trying to resolve.

The problem we are trying to address here is narrower and more immediate.

#### 2.1 Loss of author choice

`ElementInternals` removes author choice in a way that other encapsulation mechanisms do not.

With shadow DOM, authors can make an explicit tradeoff: choosing `mode: open` allows in-page accessibility testing tools to observe author-provided semantics, while `mode: closed` prioritizes encapsulation. With `ElementInternals`, there is no equivalent choice. Using it always prevents in-page tools from observing the author-provided accessibility semantics, even for authors who explicitly want their components to be testable using existing accessibility testing tools.

This makes it harder for well-intentioned authors to validate the accessibility semantics they are providing.

#### 2.2 Lack of observability for testing tools

In-page accessibility testing tools have no reliable way to determine whether a custom element uses `ElementInternals`, or whether author-provided accessibility semantics exist but are not observable.

As a result, tools cannot know when their analysis is incomplete or potentially incorrect. They also cannot reliably suppress reports that are not actionable, or inform users that a different testing context (e.g. an extension or WebDriver-based tool) may surface different results.

In practice, this leads to false positives reported against elements whose accessibility semantics are correctly defined via `ElementInternals`, but invisible to the tool. From the author’s perspective, these reports cannot be resolved: making changes does not clear them, and attempts to “fix” them may degrade the actual accessibility experience.

In CI environments, this often manifests as persistent accessibility check failures with no actionable remediation path other than disabling the accessibility tool altogether and risking missing real accessibility regressions.

---
### 3. "Wrong layer for testing"

I agree in principle that WebDriver-based approaches are the right long-term direction for accessibility testing, especially as encapsulation becomes more prevalent on the web.

Where I disagree is with the conclusion that we should therefore do nothing at the platform level _today_ to mitigate the accessibility testing regressions introduced by `ElementInternals`.

The key concern here is **backward compatibility**.

The impact here is not limited to axe-core as a single tool. Axe-core is used by a large part of the web accessibility testing **ecosystem**: many commercial and open-source tools are built on top of it, embed it, or rely on it in CI. When in-page testing becomes unreliable, that impact spreads across many tools, teams, and organizations.

Accessibility is hard to get right, even for experienced developers. I say this as someone who works full-time as a Chromium accessibility owner. Building accessible experiences – especially with custom components – requires constant checking. Automated accessibility testing is not a nice to have; it is a core part of how accessibility is maintained at scale.

The reality is that many developers do not do accessibility testing at all. Among those who do, many rely on in-page tools because they are easy to adopt and already part of their workflow. These developers are often well-intentioned and genuinely trying to do the right thing. When the current accessibility testing approach is dismissed or made less reliable without practical alternatives due to web platform primitives, the people most affected are those developers, and the result is less accessibility testing overall. The goal is to support both developers who rely on accessibility testing today and developers who want to adopt `ElementInternals`, without removing the ability to validate accessibility or discouraging testing. Providing a clear migration path is key to avoiding the perception that accessibility testing breaks as the platform evolves.

This is not an argument that in-page testing is sufficient, or that it should remain the final model. It is an argument that, given its central role today, we should avoid introducing platform features that significantly degrade its effectiveness without providing:
* a way for tools to detect when their results are incomplete, and/or
* a migration path that does not require wholesale changes to existing accessibility workflows.

Addressing these concerns does not block or delay better long-term solutions at the WebDriver layer. It helps ensure that `ElementInternals` can be adopted without unintentionally weakening accessibility practices during the transition.

---

### Proposed direction

This proposal aims to balance the encapsulation guarantees of `ElementInternals` with the practical need to preserve backward compatibility for existing accessibility testing approaches. I’d like to get concrete feedback or objections from this group on the following approach.

#### 1. Read-only reflection of ARIA set via `ElementInternals`
Expose a read-only getter on custom elements that returns a reflection of the ARIA attributes set through `ElementInternals`. This would not expose the `ElementInternals` object itself, nor allow mutation, and would be limited strictly to author-provided accessibility semantics.

```js
// Placeholder name for illustration; naming TBD.
element.getElementInternalsAria();
```

#### 2. Opt-out for authors who require full encapsulation
For authors who want strict encapsulation – including read-only access to ARIA defined via `ElementInternals` – we could provide an explicit opt-out.

For example, a property on `ElementInternals` that disables this reflection:
```js
const internals = this.attachInternals();
internals.disableAriaReflection = true;
```

This mirrors the existing pattern where authors make an explicit choice about encapsulation (similar to mode: closed for shadow roots), rather than having that choice imposed unconditionally.

#### 3. Detectability for testing tools
Finally, to support tools – especially in-page tools – in understanding their own limitations, I propose exposing a way to detect whether:
* ElementInternals is used on a custom element, and
* its accessibility semantics are intentionally not observable.

Today, tools can technically attempt to call attachInternals() on every element and infer usage based on whether it throws, but this is inefficient and fragile. Providing an explicit, read-only signal would allow tools to:
* know when their results are incomplete,
* communicate that clearly to users, and
* recommend an extension- or WebDriver-based workflow when appropriate.

Something like this:
```js
const el = document.querySelector("my-button");

// Example of a read-only signal that tools could use to understand
// whether ElementInternals is in use and whether ARIA reflection is gated.
el.elementInternalsAccessibilityInfo;
// → {
//      usesElementInternals: true,
//      ariaReflectionEnabled: false
//    }
```
This doesn’t introduce new capabilities so much as it formalizes and cleans up something that is already possible in practice.

---

The goal of this proposal is to support both:
* developers who want to adopt ElementInternals, and
* developers and tools that rely on accessibility testing today,

by providing a clear, intentional migration path rather than an abrupt loss of observability. I’m very interested in feedback on whether this direction seems reasonable, and where the concerns might be.

> This is not an argument that in-page testing is sufficient, or that it should remain the final model. It is an argument that, given its central role today, we should avoid introducing platform features that significantly degrade its effectiveness without providing:
> - a way for tools to detect when their results are incomplete, and/or
> - a migration path that does not require wholesale changes to existing accessibility workflows.

Where do we draw the line here? If we acknowledge that DOM based testing is fragile and not the future. At what point can we not worry about it.

I'm concerned that this is effectively saying we need to muddy the platform APIs with detection booleans every time we add something that might not work (but that would via web driver testing?).

referencetarget comes to mind as an example of something that will have an impact on accessibility (a very positive one), but that won't necessarily be entirely testable via the DOM.

I know you mentioned that it's not any different to closed shadow root case and if that's the case then fair, I can't remember all of the specifics.

I'm also unsure if this is actually needed? Given ElementInternals is a JS API can't you override it to intercept its use input and output? The same way you can if someone uses attach shadow with a closed shadow root (though that doesn't cover declarative shadow Dom)? It's not ideal but it would work and I think is sufficient for a testing scenario?

>> Override Element.attachElementInternals: This can only work if the tool can be loaded on the page before scripts are executed. This cannot be done reliably. Many such tools defer loading until they are needed to prevent unnecessary adding load time when they are not needed.

I see this is addressed in OP but I'm not entirely convinced by this. The tools could just load earlier right? Or is there some fundamental blocker to this?

> Opt-out for authors who require full encapsulation

Does it make sense to have an opt-out? If authors don't want this exposed sometimes then we'd realistically have to make this an opt-in because we shouldn't suddenly expose it.

If we make it opt-in then it basically defeats the entire point because many people wouldn't update their stuff to opt-in.

If this is purely about author controlled code then they could make the change but at that point why doesn't axe (etc) just agree to look at a __elementInternals property and authors can expose their element internals there?

I think we need to decide if it's okay to expose element internals (in some read-only potentially trimmed down form) by default. If any author could realistically need an opt-out of even that, then I personally think this isn't really a tenable solution.

> elementInternalsAccessibilityInfo.usesElementInternals

I'm not sure this is actually a meaningful piece of data. ElementInternals is a superset of aria properties, it includes stuff from form association, and custom state sets. It also might include a whole lot more in future.

Just because I've added a custom state to my element doesn't mean that axe can't verify it's accessibility.

@lukewarlow wrote:

> referencetarget comes to mind as an example of something that will have an impact on accessibility (a very positive one), but that won't necessarily be entirely testable via the DOM.
>
> I know you mentioned that it's not any different to closed shadow root case and if that's the case then fair, I can't remember all of the specifics.

Yes, `referencetarget` is a good example of what we'd *like* to see; it doesn't couple "the new accessibility-related feature" with "a new encapsulation boundary", it instead reuses the existing opt-in encapsulation boundary already provided by shadow DOM. That's what we're asking for, to decouple the "accessibility feature" part from the "new encapsulation boundary" part.

> I'm also unsure if this is actually needed? Given ElementInternals is a JS API can't you override it to intercept its use input and output? The same way you can if someone uses attach shadow with a closed shadow root (though that doesn't cover declarative shadow Dom)? It's not ideal but it would work and I think is sufficient for a testing scenario?
> ...
> If this is purely about author controlled code then they could make the change but at that point why doesn't axe (etc) just agree to look at a __elementInternals property and authors can expose their element internals there?

These strategies *can* work for *some* test scenarios, but there are too many exceptions for us to be able to rely on it in axe-core without breaking compatibility with a bunch of existing testing tools. The most significant examples come from axe-core-based browser extensions like Microsoft's Accessibility Insights or Deque's Axe DevTools Extension, which run axe-core from the context of a content script's isolated javascript world, where stuff like `referencetarget` works fine (because it's reflected across world boundaries via the shared DOM) but where author-implemented properties aren't visible.

> Does it make sense to have an opt-out? If authors don't want this exposed sometimes then we'd realistically have to make this an opt-in because we shouldn't suddenly expose it.
>
> If we make it opt-in then it basically defeats the entire point because many people wouldn't update their stuff to opt-in.
> ...
> I think we need to decide if it's okay to expose element internals (in some read-only potentially trimmed down form) by default. If any author could realistically need an opt-out of even that, then I personally think this isn't really a tenable solution.

I agree with this. I think if we can collectively agree on some read-only subset that's always exposed, that'd be the ideal.

I understand the desire for reading the role coming from element internals but I'm worried that either:

A) This is down to a misunderstanding of how accessible properties are computed, and how elementInternals influence those.
B) Exposing some readonly variant of element internals _will cause misunderstandings_ of how accessible properties are computed.

This isn't solely about encapsulation, but more about what the information in element internals represents, and how exposing it to tooling won't fundamentally improve the information tooling has about accessibility semantics.

To reference my earlier comment:

> I am still concerned this isn't really addressing the concrete problem statement. We're one or two steps away from "I'd like to introspect the accessible role" and into "I'd like authors to opt-out of encapsulation of internals so that I can use internals to introspect the accessible role".

I'm still unsure about the concrete problem statement here. To pull up an earlier comment:

> It is not enough for accessibility testing tools to be able to query the computed accessibility properties; we need to be able to inspect how those properties are getting their values.

With this comment and some additional comments in the thread, I understand the problem statement to be roughly: **"I would like to - in userland - read all of the information that attributes to how an accessibility property is computed so I can tell the developer which one of these is causing issues"**. Putting aside my reservations of just how daunting, complex, and ever-shifting that problem is, it's also asking for a much broader set of APIs, due to the myriad properties that influence, say, a role for example:

- `.role`
- `.elementInternals().role`
- Global styles
- Form association
- Adopted stylesheets
- `<style>` tags inside of a shadow root
- Browsers UA styles
- A user's custom userstyles
- Browser extensions with contentscripts

I'm sure there are more that I'm forgetting. So if we are to solve for that problem statement `elementInternals().role` is but one piece, should we also extend this to form association, adopted stylesheets, and styles in the ShadowDOM? 

This is also _just_ for `role`. Other properties like `aria-level` have even more complex heuristics and would require almost unfettered access to shadowdom (to, for example, find out which nodes are attributing a `headingoffset`).

However if we accept that this problem is intractable in userland, but becomes tractable in a testing environment where we have access to for e.g. WebDriver, then this becomes quite different. 

All this is to say, I think if the problem statement is as I described it, then I think we need to find some compromise in the problem statement as it's not viable for browsers to allow this. If the problem statement is different from how I described it, then please provide a concise problem statement you are trying to solve and we can work to address it.

> This isn't solely about encapsulation, but more about what the information in element internals represents, and how exposing it to tooling won't fundamentally improve the information tooling has about accessibility semantics.

@keithamus, thanks, I _think_ I understand the disagreement but let me know if I'm still missing it.

I think the key clarification is: this is about author-provided semantics, not computed semantics.

I am not trying to introspect the computed accessible role or all inputs that contribute to it. I agree that problem is intractable in userland and belongs in WebDriver / browser-internal tooling.

The concrete problem is much narrower: Allow tools to observe the author-provided accessibility semantics explicitly set via `ElementInternals`, at the same layer where tools already observe ARIA attributes today.

The accessibility testing ecosystem is layered, and different tools intentionally target different stages in the pipeline:
1. Some tools test assistive technology behavior.
2. Some test the platform accessibility tree exposed by the browser.
3. Some test the browser’s internal accessibility tree.
4. Some test what authors declared before transformations occur (DOM + ARIA + JS).

This proposal is strictly about the last layer. Tools like axe-core operate on author intent, not on final computed semantics. That’s why they inspect DOM attributes today.

@dbjorge can definitely share more about what their tool is doing today (it's nothing new, it's been the standard for years) with the author-provided accessibility properties.

Following on from todays discussion...

Both [WebAwesome](https://github.com/shoelace-style/webawesome/blob/f31ff225ba5b57e6ffcfeb35a4e36e648a2bb2ec/packages/webawesome/src/internal/webawesome-element.ts#L40) and [Lustre](https://github.com/lustre-labs/lustre/blob/6160c05c309530395b8f76aa222febbff7cdbb7e/src/lustre/runtime/client/component.ffi.mjs#L68) frameworks expose `this.internals = this.attachInternals()`. 

These are two examples of popular frameworks/libraries that already do effectively `this.attachInternals({mode:'open'})`. 

Perhaps one solution for this and for the use-cases @LeaVerou mentioned are indeed to add `{mode:'open'}` as an arg, and a `.internals` accessor. 

Perhaps one way to enforce some level of progressive disclosure could be `.attachInternals({mode:'readonly'})` which makes `.internals instanceof ReadOnlyElementInternals`. 

I'm not strictly advocating for these, but more trying to push the conversation forward with new datapoints and suggestions.

Here's the summary of the outcome of today's meeting:

> It sounds unlikely that we move forward without other non-testing related use cases for this API. Are there other scenarios that would benefit from always exposing the accessibility attributes other than accessibility testing tools?

Sure! The examples that comes to my mind right away are any browser extensions used as ATs that have any sort of behavior that's dependent on understanding the accessibility properties of elements on the page. I just looked over [the list of browser extensions that the Perkins School for the Blind provides its students](https://www.perkins.org/resource/21-chrome-extensions-struggling-students-and-special-needs/); most of the currently-maintained listings are commercial offerings, but even among the currently-maintained open source extensions on that list, you can find [an example that's trying to distinguish behavior based on role from an extension content script](https://github.com/philc/vimium/blob/5707b6ffd9d54fbf4e28bc1c8c9c6fa0adba861d/content_scripts/link_hints.js#L1137-L1160). It'd be hard to make that compatible with cases where `role` comes from `ElementInternals` without some form of browser-supported API.

This case is a good example of why we think solving this with a browser API would be preferable to solving this with something like "suggest that UI frameworks/component libraries use `this.internals = this.attachInternals()` and have tools rely on that" - that pattern doesn't cooperate very well with content script isolated world boundaries, a content script wouldn't be able to "see" `this.internals` even if a page author set it.
Browser extensions can get privileged API to solve their use case. Along with testing they don't really count. (I think they might already have access to closed shadow roots for instance.)

In that case, the best examples are probably AT bookmarklets (eg, [ReadSpeaker TextAid](https://www.readspeaker.com/solutions/text-to-speech-online/readspeaker-textaid/)) and ATs that are built to be integrated into sites by site owners (eg, [EverWay SpeechStream](https://www.everway.com/products/speechstream/)).
